label: Lost the story
title: The Biggest Loser in Show Business Is in This Mansion.
dek: Eleven of entertainment’s most famous flops, laughingstocks and has-beens walked into our mansion. We pulled their files from tax court, Congressional testimony and eighty-year-old trade papers, and behind every one we found a tax shelter, a lobbyist or a paid snitch. Then we checked this year’s news and found the same tricks still running. Only one of them lost for real. Stay with us for the final rose.
summary: A dating-show investigation of eleven famous show-business flops, from The Wicker Man to Smell-O-Vision, and who really profited from each loss.

blocks.text: Tonight: Eleven contestants. One rose. Who gets the final rose?

blocks.title: A note from the editors, who were fine before this

blocks.text: We let Jackie read the magazine. She said it was good but needed more celebrity bullshit.

We took this badly. We had just spent a hundred pages on Carthage, Napoleon, the Lost Cause and a man who fought a war against emus. We had read Hansard. We had read the Iran-Contra report, which nobody reads, including some of the people in it. What we had not given our readers was a single celebrity. No divorces. Not one person who has ever been in Us Weekly.

We told Jackie that SIDE EYE is a serious publication about who controls the historical record. Jackie asked whether the historical record includes Crazy Frog, a cartoon amphibian with no pants that once kept Coldplay from No. 1. We checked. It does.

So we did what any serious publication does when a reader is right: we pretended it was our idea. We took the same rules we used on the Roman Senate (primary sources, a scorecard, footnotes, a box at the end admitting what we can’t prove) and pointed them at show business. Celebrity bullshit, it turns out, holds up better under fact-checking than the Roman Senate does. Every single “loser” we investigated had a payday hidden somewhere. Except one.
Jackie, this one’s for you. You are not eligible for a rose.
— The Editors

Rosette: Reader of the Issue · SIDE EYE · Vol. 1 · Jackie · First Place · Celebrity B.S. Division. Ribbons: Correct, unfortunately. OFFICIAL CITATION. For being right in a way the editors found personally inconvenient. This is a rosette. You are not eligible for a rose. No cash value. Void in Carthage.
Tonight’s contestants
Eleven walked in. One rose.

rows: That Was the Week That Was
Named rock and roll. Billed for it.
Has a guy at the tabloids.
Not eligible. Too much of a winner.

blocks.text: Good evening, ladies, gentlemen, and Kevin Costner’s accountants. I’m your bachelorette, and I am here for one thing: a real loser.

Not a Biggest Loser loser. Those people get a check and a juice cleanse. And not a Bachelorette loser, sobbing in the back of a limo about “the journey.” I mean the Beck song. The genuine article. A slacker of destiny. Someone the whole world laughed at, who never got a payout, never got a comeback tour, and never got the last word.

That turns out to be shockingly hard to find. Show business is full of people the internet calls losers. Almost every one of them has a royalty check, a tax shelter, a lobbyist, or a tabloid on speed dial hidden in the glovebox.

So here are the rules. If you secretly won, you go home. If somebody else wrote your loser story so they’d look better, I’ll note it on the way out. And since most of you were famous before our readers were born, everybody gets a one-line introduction: name, rank, and what you’re famous for screwing up. And because it is 2026, every contestant must also hand me a receipt from this year: proof that their story is still happening. The last one standing gets the rose.
Gentlemen, ladies, bands. Please step out of the limo.
Round one: The flops, or who really pulled the plug
Date #1 · Bonfire night: The Wicker Man (1973)
Burned by its studio. Appraised at $5,625.

WHO? A British horror movie. A prim Scottish policeman flies to a remote island to find a missing girl, discovers a cheerful pagan cult run by Christopher Lee (Dracula himself, in a turtleneck), and spends the finale inside a giant wicker statue that is on fire. Spoiler alert, but it’s been fifty years.

THE LEGEND: The great buried masterpiece. Its studio chopped it up and dumped it as the bottom half of a double bill, and the original negative, the story goes, ended up as landfill under a British motorway. Cult-film fans have been in mourning ever since.

THE TWIST: The Wicker Man wasn’t sacrificed. It was depreciated. A New York partnership called Beachhead Properties bought the US and Canadian rights for $1.8 million: a $280,000 check plus a $1.52 million IOU that only had to be paid back if the movie made money. A flop cost the investors their cash and nothing else, while the big paper price produced big tax deductions. One investor put in $13,150 and claimed $60,194 worth of movie on his taxes. In 1988 the US Tax Court found the whole arrangement lacked economic substance and worked out what the rights to The Wicker Man were really worth: $5,625. The pagans wanted a sacrifice for a good harvest. The accountants wanted one for a good April.¹

In November 2023, Warner Bros. Discovery shelved Coyote vs. Acme, a finished Looney Tunes movie that cost about $70 million, reportedly for a tax write-off. A small distributor, Ketchup Entertainment, bought it for a reported $50 million and released it on August 28, 2026. It has made more than $100 million worldwide. Fifty years on, Hollywood is still burning finished movies for the tax man, and the coyote finally caught something.
LIMO | Made of wicker. Nobody smoke.
Date #2 · Election-night watch party: That Was the Week That Was (1964)
Satire, pre-empted by Barry Goldwater.

WHO? NBC’s American version of a hit British TV satire show, hosted by David Frost, with Alan Alda, Gloria Steinem and Tom Lehrer in the mix. Basically The Daily Show, sixty years early and with more pipe smoke.
THE LEGEND: A flop. A snooty British import that couldn’t hack it in America, crushed in the ratings by Peyton Place and gone in a season and a half.

THE TWIST: In the fall of 1964, America’s sharpest political satire kept disappearing, because Barry Goldwater’s presidential campaign kept buying its time slot. The season premiere got bumped for a Goldwater special. In October, the show was pre-empted three Tuesdays out of four. And in Los Angeles, on October 27, 1964, the half hour that replaced it was a paid political speech by a TV actor named Ronald Reagan. It was called “A Time for Choosing,” and it launched his political career. The show did eventually lose to Peyton Place fair and square. But it’s hard to build an audience when the Gipper keeps sitting in your chair.

Political airtime is being used against satire again, and this time the government is doing it. In September 2025, ABC suspended Jimmy Kimmel after FCC chairman Brendan Carr suggested stations’ licenses could be at risk, and the broadcaster Nexstar, which needed the FCC’s blessing for a merger, pre-empted the show. Same word as 1964. In January 2026, the FCC said talk-show interviews with candidates don’t automatically count as news, which drags them under the equal-time rule. In February, Stephen Colbert said CBS pulled his interview with Senate candidate James Talarico over equal-time worries (CBS says it didn’t block the interview), and Carr, calling the episode a “hoax,” said it was “one of the most fun days I’ve had in the job.” The Late Show ended in May. CBS says that was purely financial.
LIMO | Pre-empted
Date #3 · Netflix and chill, 1964: Subscription Television (1964)
Voted off the air by the ushers.

WHO? America’s first big pay-TV service, wired into homes in Los Angeles and San Francisco and run by former NBC president Pat Weaver. The main attraction was Dodgers baseball. It debuted on July 17, 1964, and the Dodgers beat the Cubs 3–2.
THE LEGEND: Proof that Americans would never pay for television. It was dead in four months.

THE TWIST: Americans didn’t reject pay TV. California’s movie theater owners got it outlawed. The Southern California Theatre Owners Association led a ballot campaign for Proposition 15, the “Free Television Act,” gathering 468,259 signatures and reportedly raising $1.5 million or more. Voters passed it in November 1964. Now read the fine print: the law banned charging for TV in your living room, but still let audiences pay to watch television in a theater, which was the theater owners’ own business. Subscription Television went dark on November 10, 1964, and filed for bankruptcy. In 1966 the California Supreme Court struck the law down as unconstitutional. By then the patient was already dead. Pay TV didn’t fail. The ushers voted it off the island.

The Dodgers eventually got their pay channel, and it went about as well. From 2014 to 2020, the team’s own SportsNet LA was blacked out across roughly half of Southern California, so fans couldn’t watch at any price. Today the channel streams straight to your phone, and the Dodgers have won back-to-back World Series, in 2024 and 2025. Pay TV was right. It was just sixty years early.
LIMO | Pay-per-view
Date #4 · Home movie night: Scophony
Invented the home theater. Owned by the movie theater.
WHO? A British company that, in the 1930s, built a TV system able to throw a picture onto a big screen. A home theater, roughly sixty years before Best Buy started selling them.
THE LEGEND: One of those dead-end gadgets from the dawn of television, filed alongside the spinning-disc TV and the steam-powered toaster. Nice try, chaps.

THE TWIST: Hollywood bought it, and according to the US government, sat on it. In December 1945 the Justice Department sued Paramount Pictures, through a wholly owned Paramount subsidiary, along with an equipment company called General Precision, whose biggest single holding, the Attorney General said, was stock in 20th Century-Fox. The charge: they had divided the world into “non-competing areas” for Scophony’s big-screen patents and used their control to suppress the technology. A Justice Department lawyer said a whole new field of public entertainment had been “unnecessarily delayed.” So the movie studios owned the rights to the one gadget that could compete with movie theaters, and the gadget went nowhere. Weird how that happens. In 1949 a settlement forced the studio-linked companies to sell their stakes. By then television had moved on without it.

On October 6, 2026, Paramount closed its roughly $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery. To get it through, it signed a settlement with 12 states promising at least 30 theatrical releases a year, each kept in theaters for at least 45 days and off subscription streaming for 90. Eighty-one years after it was accused of burying the home screen to protect the movie theaters, Paramount is now legally required to protect the movie theaters from the home screen.
LIMO | Widescreen
Round two: The airwaves, where everything is free except the things you hear
Date #5 · Sock hop: Alan Freed
He took the fall. The other DJs took promotions.
WHO? The Cleveland and New York disc jockey widely credited with popularizing the phrase “rock and roll.” In the 1950s he was the most famous DJ in America.

THE LEGEND: The face of the payola scandal, when Congress discovered in 1959 and 1960 that record companies were slipping DJs cash to play their songs. Freed was fired, charged, pleaded guilty to commercial bribery, and died broke in 1965 at 43. Rock’s founding father went down in history as rock’s first crook.

THE TWIST: Plenty of other DJs told Congress they’d taken money too, and some of them did very nicely afterward. In Boston, Joe Smith of station WILD testified that record companies had given him $8,955 over three years, though he insisted it wasn’t payola. The next year Warner Bros. Records hired him as national promotion manager, the person whose entire job is getting records played on the radio. He went on to run Warner Bros. Records, then Elektra/Asylum, and in 1986 became president of the academy that hands out the Grammys. Another Boston DJ, Norm Prescott, who had quit WBZ in 1959, admitted in closed testimony to taking $9,955.08. His old station’s general manager later said publicly that Prescott had lied in that testimony. Prescott then became a co-owner of Filmation, the cartoon studio whose Archie Show turned “Sugar, Sugar,” sung by a band of drawings, into a No. 1 hit. Freed went to court. The other guys went to work.

WBZ, Norm’s old station, now belongs to iHeartMedia. On July 9, 2026, iHeartMedia signed a consent decree with the FCC to close a payola investigation, this one into “showola,” the alleged practice of rewarding artists with airplay for playing station concerts for free. iHeart admitted no wrongdoing and no fine was announced. FCC chair Brendan Carr said “artists’ talent and the listening public should determine their success.” Sixty-six years later, Norm’s old station is the one signing the paperwork.
LIMO | With the radio on. Somebody paid for that song.
Date #6 · Ringtone karaoke: Crazy Frog
No pants. Billed weekly.

WHO? A cartoon frog in a helmet and goggles, wearing no pants, who made a noise like a revving moped. In 2005 a dance remix of the Beverly Hills Cop theme credited to him went to No. 1 in Britain and kept Coldplay off the top of the chart.
THE LEGEND: The low point of Western civilization. Grown adults still flinch at the words “ring ding ding.”

THE TWIST: The frog was a front for the landlord of the internet. The company selling him, Jamba (Jamster in some countries), had been bought in 2004 for about $273 million by VeriSign, the company that runs the .com registry. In just two weeks of May 2005, the frog’s ads ran about 42,000 times on British TV. Britain’s advertising watchdog later ruled that viewers who thought they were buying a £3 ringtone had actually signed up for £3 a week, and that the ads strongly appealed to children. It banished them to after 9 p.m. In 2006 Rupert Murdoch’s News Corp bought a majority stake. So the most annoying song of the decade was a subscription trap aimed at kids, owned first by the .com people and then by Murdoch’s News Corp. Ring ding ding, indeed.²

It took Britain more than twenty years to write the rule the frog’s ads needed. New UK subscription laws start in January 2027: renewal reminders, a cooling-off period after free trials, and easy online cancellation. America tried “click to cancel,” but a federal appeals court threw out the FTC’s rule in July 2025, and in 2026 the agency started over from scratch. The frog is still winning.
LIMO | Billed weekly
Date #7 · Open mic night: Major Bowes’ Amateurs
Gonged on air. Fed by the city.

WHO? Major Bowes’ Original Amateur Hour, the giant 1930s radio talent show. Ordinary people performed live, and if they stank, the Major banged a gong. America’s Got Talent with a bigger hammer and a Great Depression going on outside.
THE LEGEND: The gonged amateurs: the kazoo soloists, the tap dancers, the man who sang through his nose. History’s original “worst auditions” montage.

THE TWIST: The joke came with a breadline. Hopefuls poured into New York from all over the country for a shot at the show, and the ones who didn’t make it were stranded. In September 1935 alone, some 1,200 of them turned to New York City relief stations for food and shelter. The ones who did get on the air were paid $10 an appearance. By 1936 the Major was reportedly grossing $30,000 a week. The losers weren’t the people who got gonged. They were the people who paid their own bus fare to audition for a millionaire.

A 2024 class action over Beast Games, MrBeast’s competition show on Amazon Prime Video, alleges contestants were really employees under California law and weren’t properly paid. Ninety years later, the gong is an algorithm, and the bus fare is still on you.
LIMO | Gonged
Round three: The gossip pages (Jackie, this is your part)
Date #8 · Dinner and a movie: Katharine Hepburn
Box office poison. Four Oscars.
WHO? The brainy, trouser-wearing movie star who went on to win four Best Actress Oscars, still the record.

THE LEGEND: In May 1938 a full-page ad in The Hollywood Reporter, headlined “WAKE UP! HOLLYWOOD PRODUCERS,” branded a list of stars “box office poison”: Hepburn, Greta Garbo, Joan Crawford, Marlene Dietrich, Mae West and more. Hepburn’s studio, RKO, offered her a B picture called Mother Carey’s Chickens. She refused it and paid $75,000 to buy her way out of her contract. Actors have been terrified of the phrase ever since.

THE TWIST: The ad was signed by Harry Brandt, president of the Independent Theatre Owners Association, speaking as the voice of the little guy who runs the neighborhood movie house. Two years later, the trade paper Harrison’s Reports printed charges from a rival exhibitors’ leader, Abram Myers, that Brandt now co-owned a film company with an RKO executive and had a deal to produce two Charles Boyer pictures for RKO, after Brandt had testified he had no connection with any producer or distributor. So RKO collected $75,000 to let its “poison” walk out the door, and the man who poisoned her ended up making movies for RKO. When The Philadelphia Story became a hit in 1940, Brandt sent Hepburn a telegram: “Come on back, Katie. All is forgiven.” Forgiven. By him.

The theater owners never stopped telling Hollywood what to do. Myers’s old group, Allied, merged into the National Association of Theatre Owners, which renamed itself Cinema United in March 2025. In February 2026 it told a Senate subcommittee that a Netflix deal for Warner Bros. would be “economically and culturally catastrophic.” In April it pressed studios to keep movies in theaters for at least 45 days. (Scroll back up to Scophony to see how that turned out.) The poison-pen lobby is still in business. These days it picks on streaming.
LIMO | Box office
Date #9 · Drinks, off the record: Francesca De Scaffa
Joke divorcée. Chief snitch.
WHO? A Venezuelan-born B-movie actress and ex-wife of Bruce Cabot, the hero of the original King Kong.

THE LEGEND: The tabloid joke divorcée. Wire photos from 1951 show her laughing in court as her divorce came through. Later she married a Mexican bullfighter, and that marriage was annulled the same year. Filed under: gold digger, washed up.

THE TWIST: She was the snitch. Confidential, the 1950s scandal magazine that sold millions of copies of Hollywood dirt, needed people inside the parties, and its editor, Howard Rushmore, called De Scaffa “our chief Hollywood source.” She bragged that she “had access to almost every home in Hollywood,” and she reportedly sold the magazine stories about men she had been involved with herself. After one of her stories triggered a lawsuit, Rushmore testified, she changed her story and admitted she “had not been present.” In 1957 she was one of 11 people indicted in California’s criminal libel case against the magazine. She hid out in Mexico City and was deported to Cuba as “an undesirable visitor.” Then the punchline took a bow. She married Raymond Offroy, the French ambassador to Mexico appointed by Charles de Gaulle, who later sat in France’s National Assembly as a Gaullist deputy. Hollywood’s top rat ended up as a French politician’s wife. Bruce Cabot fought a giant ape. She got the better ending.

The tabloid source is still the most valuable person in the room, and still the shakiest. In 2026 Prince Harry, Elton John and five others took the publisher of the Daily Mail to trial in London, accusing it of unlawfully gathering private information. A private investigator, Gavin Burrows, whose 2021 statement describing phone hacking was central to the claimants’ case, told the court in March that he never wrote it and that his signature was forged. (The claimants’ lawyer called the forgery claim “wild and unsubstantiated.”) Seventy years later, the source is still saying he was never really there.
LIMO | To Paris
Hometown dates: The final two
Two contestants are left in the mansion. One of them is hiding something. The other one is the genuine article.
Hometown date · Press junket: Barbara Payton
The tabloids’ favorite victim. Also a vendor.
WHO? A blonde 1950s movie actress who starred opposite James Cagney and Gregory Peck.

THE LEGEND: The textbook starlet the tabloids ate alive. In 1951 her two boyfriends, the actors Franchot Tone and Tom Neal, got into a fistfight over her, and Neal put Tone in a coma. After that came B-movies, scandal, arrests and an early death at 39 in 1967. Every Hollywood cautionary tale about the gossip machine has her picture in it.

THE TWIST: She was also a supplier. According to Confidential’s own publisher, Robert Harrison, Payton would stop by the magazine’s Hollywood office “and sell a story whenever she was short of cash.” The gossip machine’s favorite victim was also on its vendor list. We’re not saying she wasn’t a victim. She was. She was also an invoice.

In July 2026, a London judge threw out Prince Harry’s case against the Daily Mail’s publisher, ruling it was “not a permissible approach” to argue that a story “must have been unlawfully sourced.” The paper’s defense was that its stories came from the stars’ own friends, aides and publicists. In August the judge ordered the claimants to pay an initial £9.5 million in legal costs. Barbara could have saved them the money. In Hollywood, the call is usually coming from inside the house.
LIMO | And she’s tipping off the photographers on the way out
Hometown date · Dinner and a smell: Smell-O-Vision (1960)
Thirty smells. All of them late.

WHO? The only feature film ever shown in Smell-O-Vision: Scent of Mystery, a travel mystery produced by Mike Todd Jr., son of the showman behind Around the World in 80 Days. Pipes under the seats released thirty smells on cue. Elizabeth Taylor, his stepmother, turns up in a cameo. Eddie Fisher, her husband, sang the title song.

THE LEGEND: The most famous flop in the history of the nose. Variety called the fight with a rival system “the battle of the smellies.” In theaters, the smells came out of the vents with a hiss, reached the balcony a few seconds late and hung around into the next scene. Henny Youngman reportedly said, “I didn’t understand the picture. I had a cold.” On a reported $2 million budget, it took in about $300,000 in North American rentals. No feature film has used the process since.

rows: That Was the Week That Was

blocks.text: Two left. One rose.
Coming up… The final rose. Stay with us.
The Final Rose
Live · The final rose · This portion of the program was not scripted

Here’s who didn’t lose: Mike Todd Jr. His father had left him the rights to Around the World in 80 Days, which he controlled mostly with Elizabeth Taylor. “Dad left me in the fortunate position of being able to do more or less what I want,” he told Roger Ebert.
LIMO | Around the world

The man who lost is listed in the credits as “Osmologist.” Hans Laube was a former advertising executive from Zurich who had started out designing a way to clear stale air out of auditoriums. If he could take smells out of a theater, he figured, he could pipe them in. He had been trying to make movies smell for twenty years. He showed a system he called Scentovision at the New York World’s Fair in 1939 and 1940. In 1943 the New York Times reported that it “produced odors as quickly and easily as the soundtrack of a film produces sound.” Nobody in Hollywood or television wanted it. In 1946 he went back to Europe.
Then Mike Todd Jr. called. He would make the movie on one condition: Scentovision had to be renamed Smell-O-Vision.

Then Laube lost the race. A rival producer, Walter Reade Jr., opened a smell movie of his own, Behind the Great Wall in “AromaRama,” in New York on December 9, 1959. Scent of Mystery premiered in Chicago on January 6, 1960. Twenty years of work, beaten by four weeks.
Then he lost the reviews. His own director, Jack Cardiff, said the smells “were exactly like cheap eau-de-Cologne,” and later called Laube a “phony gentleman” and “a fake.”

Then he lost the money. “He lost all his money, my mom went to work, and he died about 16 years later, penniless and broken,” his daughter, Carmen Laube, said. He kept inventing, first in a lab on East 84th Street, then at the family’s kitchen table. His next product was BestAir, an electronic room fragrancer that, his daughter says, came before Glade. It went nowhere. He died in New York in 1976.

Now look around this mansion. Every other contestant had something going for them. The Wicker Man had a tax shelter. Pay TV had the Dodgers’ back-to-back rings coming. Scophony’s old owner got a merger. The payola guys got promoted. The frog got Murdoch. Hepburn got four Oscars and a telegram of forgiveness. Francesca got a French deputy. Barbara got paid. Even Mike Todd Jr. got Around the World in 80 Days.

Hans Laube got a screen credit nobody could pronounce and a smell that arrived late. Nobody conned him. Nobody framed him. He had a strange idea, he believed in it for twenty years, he bet everything on it, and the whole world laughed at the result, which really was as bad as they said. No write-off, no consent decree, no job in promotion. He is the only contestant here who lost exactly the way the story says he did.

Smell-O-Vision finally works. It just needed a bigger room. In August 2025 the Las Vegas Sphere opened an AI-expanded Wizard of Oz with wind, fog and smells; its president had teased a smell-o-vision moment during the tornado. In September 2026 it added “themed scents,” including falling apples that now smell like apples. The show has sold more than four million tickets, and Sphere’s Las Vegas business still posted an operating loss of $69.6 million in the second quarter of 2026. Laube didn’t need a better nose. He needed someone else’s money.
Beck wrote the anthem in 1993. Hans Laube had been living it since 1960.
Hans Laube, will you accept this rose?
(No answer. He died in 1976. Somewhere, very faintly, there is a smell of cheap cologne, arriving a few seconds late.)

blocks.title: What we can prove / what we can’t

blocks.text: Proven:

items: The Wicker Man: Beachhead Properties’ $280,000 check and $1.52 million nonrecourse note; the Tax Court’s 1988 finding that the activity lacked economic substance; the $5,625 valuation (Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1988-238).
That Was the Week That Was was pre-empted by paid Goldwater broadcasts, including, in Los Angeles on October 27, 1964, Reagan’s “A Time for Choosing.”
Proposition 15 passed in 1964, allowed pay TV in theaters, and was struck down in Weaver v. Jordan (1966); Subscription Television shut down and filed for bankruptcy.
The Justice Department sued Paramount and General Precision over Scophony’s patents in 1945; a 1949 consent judgment forced them to sell their stakes.
Joe Smith’s and Norm Prescott’s payola testimony and their later careers; iHeartMedia’s July 2026 FCC consent decree.
VeriSign’s 2004 purchase of Jamba; the Advertising Standards Authority’s 2005 ruling on the Crazy Frog ads.
Some 1,200 rejected Amateur Hour hopefuls sought New York City relief in September 1935.
The 1938 “box office poison” ad and Hepburn’s $75,000 buyout.
De Scaffa’s role as Confidential’s “chief Hollywood source,” her indictment and deportation, and her later marriage to Raymond Offroy.
Behind the Great Wall in AromaRama opened December 9, 1959; Scent of Mystery premiered in Smell-O-Vision on January 6, 1960. Laube showed Scentovision at the 1939–40 New York World’s Fair.
The 2026 Daily Mail trial, its dismissal, and the costs order.

blocks.text: Likely:

items: Brandt’s RKO ties. Harrison’s Reports printed the charges in 1940; we have not found Brandt’s response.
That De Scaffa sold stories about her own lovers (reported).
Payton’s story-selling, on publisher Robert Harrison’s own account, as quoted in Harold Conrad’s 1982 memoir.
News Corp’s 2006 majority stake in Jamba; the size of the Proposition 15 war chest; Major Bowes’ $30,000 a week.
Laube’s losses, on his daughter’s account; Scent of Mystery’s $2 million budget and $300,000 in rentals; Henny Youngman’s quip.
That Coyote vs. Acme was shelved for a tax write-off (widely reported; the studio never said so in those words).

blocks.text: What we are not claiming:

items: That Brandt’s 1938 ad was planted by a studio. We found the conflict of interest, not the order.
That Scophony’s technology would have succeeded. The government alleged suppression; the case was settled, never tried.
That the pre-emptions killed That Was the Week That Was. It also lost the ratings fight.
That CBS ended The Late Show for political reasons. CBS says the decision was financial.
That Laube was paid nothing. We found no record of his deal with Todd; his daughter’s account is our evidence.

blocks.text: The other side. Plenty of these really did fail. The Wicker Man was butchered in the edit, That Was the Week That Was lost to Peyton Place, and pay TV in 1964 was clunky and expensive. Our point is narrower: in every case, the loser label stuck to the face on the poster, while the accountants, lobbyists, sponsors and snitches behind it walked out the side door, and most of them are still in business.
Notes
¹ The Tax Court also hit the investor with a $5,000 penalty for dragging the case out. [E.G.] · The tax man always gets his sacrifice. [H.C.]
² The song itself is a remix of the Beverly Hills Cop theme. Somebody should check Eddie Murphy’s royalty statements. [H.C.] · Please don’t. [E.G.]
